papers.title: Navigating Gestational Health in the Reddit Pregnancy Community: A Mixed-Methods Study of Online Peer Discourse and Embodied Experience
papers.abstract: Background: While health behaviours and clinical markers such as gestational weight gain GWG), physical activity, and nutrition are critical for optimizing maternal and fetal outcomes, pregnant individuals often face a fragmented informational landscape characterized by a heavy burden of clinical restrictions. Consequently, many turn to online, pseudo-anonymous communities like Reddit to crowdsource support, share experiences, and navigate complex health decisions outside the formal clinical encounter. This study aimed to examine how pregnant individuals utilize the Reddit community r/Pregnant to seek health-related information, navigate clinical recommendations surrounding GWG and health-related behaviours, and share lived experiences. Methods: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study design was employed, combining computational topic modeling and qualitative analysis. In aim 1, all public posts published on the r/Pregnant subreddit between 2009 and 2024 were analyzed using BERTopic, a transformer-based modeling framework, to map the landscape of discourse and identify health-related topics. In aim 2, nine health-related topics were purposively selected, and 700 high-engagement posts (ranked by comment volume) across topics were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, following Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework. Results: BERTopic identified 90 distinct pregnancy-related topics across 15 years of discourse. Nine were health-related and selected for analysis, with gestational weight gain having the highest volume (Rank 14; 2,241 posts). Reflexive thematic analysis generated five overarching themes: (1) Reddit as a Site of Collective Sense-Making; (2) Decision-Making Under Uncertainty; (3) The Emotional Burden of Maternal Responsibility; (4) Embodied Knowledge in Practice; and (5) Social Pressure and Autonomy. Conclusions: A substantial gap exists between standardized prenatal clinical guidelines and the lived, physical reality of pregnancy. Pregnant individuals actively use digital peer support to adapt clinical advice, cope with weight-related stigma, and exercise autonomy. These findings highlight the importance of strengthening prenatal healthcare communication through more empathetic, non-judgmental, and individualized approaches that better reflect pregnant individuals concerns and lived experiences.

papers.title: Bacterial Sexually Transmitted Infections and Oral HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Use in HVTN 704/HPTN 085
papers.abstract: Objectives: To describe bacterial STI burden and examine its association with time-varying oral PrEP use among participants in a multinational HIV prevention efficacy trial. Methods: We conducted a post-hoc analysis of HVTN 704/HPTN 085 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02716675), a randomized, placebo-controlled study of the VRC01 broadly neutralizing antibody for HIV prevention. Men and transgender persons who have sex with men were enrolled in Brazil, Peru, United States, and Switzerland (April 2016-October 2018). All participants received an enhanced prevention package including STI testing every six months and optional access to oral PrEP. Prevalence and incidence of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis were described. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations between time-varying PrEP use and incident STIs. Results: Among 2,687 participants, 27.9% had a bacterial STI at enrollment (chlamydia 11.1%, gonorrhea 10.2%, syphilis 13.1%). Prevalence was higher in Brazil (36.7%) and Peru (34.9%) than in the United States/Switzerland (21.4%). Rectal and oropharyngeal infections predominated. Among participants negative at baseline, incidence of any bacterial STI was 29.4 per 100 person-years (95% CI: 27.2-31.7). Incidence was higher during periods of PrEP use than non-use (HR 1.75, 95% CI: 1.44-2.13), consistent across pathogens. Conclusions: In this multinational HIV prevention trial, bacterial STI burden was high, particularly in Latin America and at extragenital sites. STI incidence was higher during periods of reported oral PrEP use. These findings highlight the importance of integrating multisite STI testing, treatment, counseling, and targeted prevention into HIV prevention services and future efficacy trials.

papers.title: Changes in antimicrobial susceptibility after six months of doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis: results from a single center, open label, uncontrolled clinical trial (the SafeDoxyPEP trial)
papers.abstract: Synopsis BackgroundDoxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP) reduces the incidence of bacterial sexually transmitted infections, but its impact on antimicrobial susceptibility among bystander bacteria remains unclear. ObjectivesTo assess changes in susceptibility to doxycycline among rectal Escherichia coli after 6 months of doxyPEP. Secondary objectives assessed susceptibility for other classes of antimicrobials and in other species. Patients and methodsSingle-centre, open-label, single-arm trial at an HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis clinic in Belgium. Participants used doxycycline 200mg within 72h after condomless sex for 180 days. Anorectal swabs and oral rinse samples were collected at baseline and day 180. Susceptibility was assessed by disc diffusion on six colonies per species. Differences in inhibition-zone diameters were analysed using censored Bayesian mixed-effects Gaussian regression. ResultsSeventy-nine participants were enrolled, 73 completed day 180. Among rectal isolates, cefixime inhibition-zone diameters decreased in E. coli and Klebsiella spp., other estimates were imprecise. Among oral isolates, inhibition-zone diameters decreased for doxycycline and azithromycin in streptococci, staphylococci and commensal Neisseria spp.; ceftriaxone and cefixime in commensal Neisseria spp.; and ciprofloxacin and penicillin in staphylococci and commensal Neisseria spp. Ceftriaxone inhibition-zone diameters increased in oral streptococci. Sensitivity analyses were broadly consistent. Twenty-five participants experienced drug-related adverse events, none serious. ConclusionsSix months of doxyPEP was associated with reduced susceptibility to doxycycline and several other antimicrobials, predominantly among oral bacteria. Rectal findings were less precise apart from reduced cefixime susceptibility in E. coli and Klebsiella spp. These findings support further studies of DoxyPEP and bystander selection across multiple bacterial taxa and antimicrobial classes.

papers.title: Paired molecular characterization of repeat Chlamydia trachomatis infection among pregnant women in East London, South Africa
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Repeat Chlamydia trachomatis positivity after treatment may reflect persistent infection, reinfection, or residual nucleic acid. We compared paired ompA genotypes of C. trachomatis in pregnant women in South Africa and assessed macrolide resistance-associated mutations. Methods: We analyzed paired baseline and follow-up specimens from 43 pregnant women with C. trachomatis detected at two study visits. We determined ompA genotypes by PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing and compared genotypes between visits. A fragment of the 23S rRNA gene was sequenced to identify selected macrolide resistance-associated mutations. Results: At baseline, ompA typing was successful in 38/43 (88%) specimens and 36/43 (84%) at follow-up, with paired genotype results available for 32 women (74%). Genotypes E, J and D predominated at baseline and follow-up. The same genotype was detected at both visits in 22/32 women (69%), whereas 10/32 (31%) had a different genotype at follow-up. Genotype concordance was observed in 2/2 (100%) women with paired results at the test-of-cure visit, 13/16 (81%) assessed at 32 weeks gestation, and 7/14 (50%) assessed postnatally. No targeted macrolide resistance associated mutations were detected in specimens with successful 23S rRNA sequencing. Conclusions: One-third of women with paired results had a different ompA genotype at follow-up, consistent with acquisition of a different strain after treatment. Concordant ompA genotypes may reflect persistence or reinfection with a strain sharing the same genotype, acquired from the same or a different partner. Macrolide resistance associated mutations were not detected. High-resolution typing methods would allow more detailed understanding of persistent C. trachomatis test positivity in this population.

papers.title: Adherence to iron and folic acid supplementation among pregnant women in rural areas of Eastern Tigray, Ethiopia: A community-based study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPoor adherence to Iron and folic acid (IFA) remains major public health challenge in Ethiopia. While national protocols advise IFA supplementation during pregnancy, adherence is low in the nation particularly in rural areas. In the study setting, there is lack of updated data regarding adherence to IFA and its determinant factors among pregnant women. ObjectiveTo assess adherence to IFA supplements and associated factors among pregnant women in rural setting of Eastern Tigray, Ethiopia, 2025. MethodsA community-based cross-sectional study was carried out from March 2025 to April 2025 among 614 pregnant women in Eastern Tigray, Ethiopia. Simple random and systematic random sampling techniques were utilized to select districts and study participants respectively. Data analysis was performed using SPSS 25, employing both binary and multivariable logistic regression. Multi-collinearity and goodness of fit tests were ensured using the variance inflation factor and Hosmer-Lemeshow test respectively. Statistical significance was declared at a p-value less than 0.05. ResultsA total of 599 participants were included and the prevalence of adherence to IFA Supplementation (IFAS) was 56% (95% CI: 52%, 60%). Having [≥] 4 ANC visits (AOR= 37.7 95% CI: 14.08 - 101.03), mothers with previous history of anemia (AOR=2.2 CI: 1.07 - 4.69), age of mothers [≥] 40 years (AOR= 11.5 CI: 1.06 - 124.05), mothers who received counseling about IFAS (AOR, 7.1; CI 3.24 - 15.37), and mothers travelled to the health facility 30 to 60 minutes and more than 60 minutes (AOR, 0.02; CI 0.01 - 0.04), and (AOR, 0.01(0 - 0.004), respectively had statistically significant association with adherence to IFAS. ConclusionWomen having four or more ANC visits, previous history of anemia, receiving counseling about IFAS, elder age, and travelling less than 60 minutes to seek healthcare were associated with increased odds of adherence to IFAS.

papers.title: Portable gynaecological imaging to enhance naked-eye visual assessment for the management of cervical precancer among women living with HIV in Kenya: An implementation-informed, diagnostic accuracy study protocol
papers.abstract: BackgroundCervical cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries, particularly among women living with HIV (WLHIV). Although visual-based assessment in primary care is feasible and facilitates same-day management, its diagnostic accuracy is dependent on provider experience and skill, resulting in variable performance. Portable gynecological imaging may enhance visual assessment while supporting implementation of cervical cancer prevention in primary care. MethodsWe will conduct a cross-sectional study among 150 WLHIV co-infected with human papillomavirus and their healthcare providers at Molo Sub-County Hospital in Nakuru County, Kenya. The study will evaluate the agreement between portable gynecological imaging-enhanced visual assessment and conventional colposcopy; estimate diagnostic accuracy using histopathology as the reference standard; determine provider-level acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility, and assess patient-level satisfaction using validated instruments complemented by qualitative interviews and integrated using a sequential, explanatory, mixed-methods approach. DiscussionThis study will generate preliminary evidence on the diagnostic accuracy and implementation of portable gynecological imaging in primary care. If shown to be accurate, acceptable, appropriate, and feasible, portable gynecological imaging could improve timely identification and management of cervical precancer, and support expansion of high-quality cervical cancer prevention services in similar resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Cervicovaginal metabolites mediate the relationship between vaginal microbiota and risk for Chlamydia trachomatis infection
papers.abstract: BackgroundChlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infection and a cause of adverse reproductive outcomes. Epidemiologic studies describe bacterial vaginosis (BV) as a major risk factor for CT infection. Emerging data suggest that BV-associated bacteria and their metabolites contribute to CT susceptibility. Here, we measured the role of specific bacteria in incident CT and evaluated a hypothesized causal role between the vaginal microbiota, its metabolites, and CT risk. MethodsWe conducted a nested case-control study of Kenyan women who engage in transactional sex from the Mombasa Cohort who acquired CT versus those who did not, and compared their vaginal microbiome and metabolome at the visit preceding CT acquisition. We determined CT infection and total bacterial load using qPCRs. 16S rRNA sequencing was used to characterize the genital microbiome, and BV status was determined using Nugent-Hillier and Amsel scoring criteria. Metabolites were measured using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from a subset of women. FindingsWomen with BV, high vaginal microbial diversity, and community state types III and IV were significantly more likely to have CT at their next visit. CT infection itself did not alter vaginal microbial diversity. More specifically, both concentrations and relative abundances of Lactobacillus crispatus and several BV-associated bacteria (Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella/Prevotella timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum) were predictive of CT outcomes. Vaginal metabolites differed between cases and controls pre-CT, including Tyramine, reduced and oxidized Glutathione, and sucrose. In a mediation analysis, the vaginal metabolome significantly mediated the relationship between the microbiome and CT infection. InterpretationWe show for the first time that the association between BV and CT risk is mediated by differences in the metabolome. Identification of the mechanisms underlying increased CT risk with BV can inform interventions to reduce infections in high-risk women. FundingUS NIH (R01AI13214401-A1) Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSChlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection globally and can lead to serious adverse health outcomes. Previous studies have pointed to an association between the vaginal microbiota composition, particularly the presence of bacterial vaginosis (BV)-associated taxa, and chlamydia susceptibility. However, most studies have been cross-sectional, measuring the microbiome at the time of infection. The few longitudinal studies specifically assessing the microbiome dynamics preceding CT infection have generally been limited by small sample sizes or infrequent sampling. Further, the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear. Added value of this studyIn this nested case-control study, we evaluated the vaginal microbiome preceding CT acquisition and compared participants who subsequently acquired infection with matched controls who remained uninfected. We found that women who acquired CT had a significantly higher vaginal microbial diversity in the past 1-2 months, while the CT infection itself did not lead to broad changes in the microbiome, suggesting directionality to this relationship. Participants who acquired CT were >2-fold more likely to have BV by Nugent-Hillier or Amsel criteria at the previous visit. Having a diverse community state type IV was associated with the strongest likelihood of CT acquisition. More specifically, women who acquired CT were more likely to have a microbiome characterized by the depletion of Lactobacillus crispatus and higher abundances of Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella (Prevotella) timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum. To assess the possible mechanism through which the microbiome influenced CT risk, we measured the cervicovaginal metabolome in a subset of participants. We found that 70% of the effect of the vaginal microbiome on CT acquisition risk could be explained by the metabolome, highlighting the role of bacterial metabolites in CT susceptibility. Overall, by focusing on samples collected prior to infection acquisition, with a short period between visits, our study contributes robust temporal evidence that the vaginal microbiome impacts CT susceptibility rather than simply being correlated, with the presence of CT, with metabolites potentially playing a key role in this relationship. Implications of all the available evidenceOur findings support the concept that the vaginal microbiome is a potentially modifiable risk factor for CT acquisition, with specific BV-associated bacteria, alongside L. crispatus depletion, identified as key modulators of risk. This study is a step towards confirming the directionality of the microbiome-CT infection relationship and establishing potential mechanisms through which the microbiome influences CT risk. These findings, along with previous literature, have the potential to lead to microbiome or metabolite-targeted interventions that would reduce the risk of CT acquisition.

papers.title: Mobile money vendors as a community channel for adolescent condom provision and sexual health information in Uganda: a type-II hybrid effectiveness-implementation study
papers.abstract: PurposeUnmarried adolescents in Uganda have limited access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, and conventional programs have struggled to reach them sustainably. Mobile money vendors (MMVs) are ubiquitous in young peoples daily lives. We assessed the feasibility of an MMV-based intervention to provide condoms and SRH information to adolescents. MethodsIn this type-II hybrid effectiveness-implementation study in Eastern Uganda, 30 MMVs provided oral and printed information, free condoms, and referrals for four months in 2024. Feasibility was assessed using the Bowen framework, drawing on service logs, baseline and endline surveys of adolescents aged 15-19 years (n = 1,204), three focus group discussions with MMVs, eight key informant interviews, a post-intervention MMV survey, and supervision reports. ResultsMMVs recorded 104,849 adolescent customer visits; oral information was provided at 54,365 visits and condoms at 21,056 visits. Condom use in the intervention arm increased from 67.3% to 77.7% (p = 0.04), and the proportion obtaining condoms from MMVs rose from 0% to 64.6%. Adolescents valued the services convenience and confidentiality. Initial resistance from some community adults largely diminished, although referrals remained few (210 cases). All MMV shops completed the intervention without disrupting business, and customer numbers and sales rose 1.64- and 1.50-fold. Suggested adaptations included vendor identification and services for girls, integration with public health systems for scalability. ConclusionsThe MMV-based approach was feasible and reached hard-to-access unmarried adolescents with condoms and SRH information. For scale-up, improvements for adaptation and large-scale evaluation are necessary. Trial registrationUMIN000053332

papers.title: Barriers and facilitators to cervical precancer treatment adherence among women in Harare, Zimbabwe: A qualitative study
papers.abstract: Adherence to recommended treatment after a positive cervical screening result remains suboptimal in Zimbabwe. This study explored how women interpreted a cervical precancer diagnosis and how emotional, interpersonal, economic, and health-system factors shaped treatment decisions. We conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 25 purposively selected women aged 25-50 years who had screened positive by visual inspection with acetic acid and were recommended for ablative or excisional treatment at two high-volume clinics in Harare. The qualitative component drew on the Health Belief Model and a phenomenological orientation to lived experience. Data were examined using combined deductive and inductive thematic analysis. Three interrelated themes were identified. First, women initially interpreted precancer through fear, shock, and uncertainty; misconceptions that precancer meant invasive cancer, infertility, or imminent death could delay action, whereas clear counselling reframed the diagnosis as treatable. Second, multilevel conditions shaped adherence. Supportive health workers, partner or family encouragement, prior awareness, and connection to HIV services facilitated treatment, while indirect costs, transport, fragmented referral pathways, scheduled excisional services, inconsistent communication, partner opposition, and sexual coercion impeded care. Third, Health Belief Model constructs operated in both directions: perceived severity motivated action when paired with credible benefits and self-efficacy, but produced avoidance when amplified by misinformation and weak support. Improving treatment completion will require standardised counselling, reliable navigation and follow-up, more accessible excisional services, and interventions that address partner dynamics and indirect costs. Screening scale-up should be matched by timely treatment capacity so that women with positive results complete the prevention pathway.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Gynecologic Disorders and Adult-Onset Psychiatric Conditions: Integrating Matched Cohort, Polygenic Risk Score, and Mendelian Randomization
papers.abstract: BackgroundEndometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and uterine fibroids are linked to psychiatric morbidity, but evidence on causality across the full psychiatric spectrum remains limited. MethodsWe assessed associations between endometriosis, PCOS, uterine fibroids and adult- onset psychiatric conditions (schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, mood disorders, anxiety and stress-related disorders) in UK Biobank female participants using three complementary approaches: a matched-pair cohort design, a polygenic risk score (PRS)-based cohort analysis, and bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR). Sensitivity analyses were performed to test robustness. ResultsEndometriosis was associated with mood disorders (OR= 1.51, 95% CI 1.40, 1.63), anxiety and stress-related disorders (OR=1.49, 95% CI 1.38, 1.62), and behavioral syndromes with physical components (OR= 1.28, 95% CI 1.01, 1.62). Uterine fibroids were associated with mood disorders (OR=1.17; 95% CI 1.11, 1.23), anxiety and stress-related disorders (OR=1.40, 95% CI 1.34, 1.48), and behavioral syndromes (OR=1.29, 95% CI 1.12, 1.48). PCOS was associated with mood disorders (OR=1.47, 95% CI 1.32, 1.64) and anxiety and stress-related disorders (OR=1.79, 95% CI 1.62,1.99), but not behavioral syndromes. No gynecologic disorder was associated with schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders. Genetic analyses supported shared liability and causal effects between fibroids and anxiety disorders. ConclusionsWomen with gynecologic disorders are at increased risk of mood and anxiety- and stress-related disorders, and those with endometriosis or fibroids also face additional risk of behavioral syndromes. At least some of these risks appear driven by genetic liability, supporting routine mental health screening in gynecologic care and integrated treatment of gynecologic and mental health. Key MessagesO_LIWomen with endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, or uterine fibroids have 17-80% higher risks of mood and anxiety/stress-related disorders but not psychotic disorders. C_LIO_LIGenetic analyses support shared genetic liability between uterine fibroids and psychiatric disorders, with evidence for a causal effect of fibroids on anxiety disorders. C_LIO_LIThese findings support integrating routine mental health screening into gynecologic care for affected women. C_LI

papers.title: Sexual and Relationship Content Exposure on Social Media and Adolescent Sexual Health Attitudes
papers.abstract: PurposeTo identify patterns of adolescents reported exposure to sexual and relationship content on social media and examine their associations with permissive sexual attitudes and perceived barriers to condom use. MethodsIn a cross-sectional online survey (January to February 2026), 1,124 US high school students aged 16 to 18 years rated their typical exposure to 20 content categories developed with Youth Advisory Board input. Network analysis identified content communities, latent profile analysis grouped adolescents by community-level exposure, and covariate-adjusted linear models compared attitudes across profiles. ResultsFour content communities and 4 exposure profiles were identified. Adolescents in the High Overall Exposure profile (n = 299; 27.3%) reported frequent exposure across all content communities and had higher adjusted permissive sexual attitudes (difference, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.75; d = 0.69) and perceived condom-use barriers (difference, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.31 to 0.69; d = 0.61) than the Moderate General Exposure profile. Differences were attenuated but persisted after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, sensation seeking, religiosity, and social media time (0.39 and 0.38) and were robust to data-quality exclusions and correction for classification error. DiscussionAdolescents exposure to sexual and relationship content on social media is patterned, and higher overall exposure is associated with attitudes relevant to condom use. Sexual health counseling may benefit from addressing the broader mix of messages adolescents encounter online. Implications and ContributionAdolescents reported exposure to sexual and relationship content on social media formed distinct patterns. Higher overall exposure, particularly to sexual rather than relationship-focused content, was associated with more permissive sexual attitudes and greater perceived condom-use barriers, suggesting that sexual health counseling should consider adolescents online content environments.

papers.title: Seek and You Will Find: A Prospective Case-Finding Study for the Detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae Xpert(R) CT/NG Diagnostic Escape Mutants in England
papers.abstract: ObjectivesIn 2025, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), confirmed the identification of a Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) diagnostic escape mutant for the Xpert(R) CT/NG assay (Cepheid). Subsequently, a small number of further mutants were reported internationally. The assay comprises two NG-specific targets, NG2 and NG4, and amplification is required in both to report a positive result. This prospective case-finding study aimed to investigate the presence of diagnostic escape mutants in NG-negative specimens from two sexual health services using the Xpert(R) CT/NG assay to provide in-clinic testing. MethodsResidual Xpert(R) NG-negative clinical specimens were collected during December 2025 and transferred to the national STI Reference Laboratory at UKHSA. Following anonymisation extracts were tested on the GeneProof Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR kit (GeneProof). GeneProof NG-positive specimens were re-tested on the Xpert(R) CT/NG assay to confirm. ResultsIn total, 978 specimens were tested on the GeneProof assay; 99.7% (975/978) were confirmed as NG-negative. Three specimens (two rectal swabs and one urine sample) tested NG-positive on the GeneProof assay. Two specimens were re-tested on the Xpert(R) CT/NG assay, both re-tested NG-negative. Both samples amplified either the NG2 or NG4 target within the Xpert(R) NG assay, but not both targets required for a positive result. The remaining sample was insufficient for re-testing. An extrapolation of possible missed NG cases due to mutants, indicated that between 62 and 562 cases may have been missed in 2025 from these clinics. ConclusionsThis prospective case-finding study demonstrated excellent sensitivity of the Xpert(R) CT/NG assay with 99.7% of NG-negative samples correctly identified. However, a small number of diagnostic escape mutants were detected, and extrapolation suggests there may be some degree of missed cases from providers using this assay as a near-patient test. Further work is required to fully understand the prevalence of the mutants and clinical implications of missed diagnoses. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topic?C_ST_ABSNeisseria gonorrhoeae diagnostic escape mutants for the Xpert(R) CT/NG assay (Cepheid), lacking one or both diagnostic targets, have recently been identified in England and internationally. However, the true prevalence of these mutants and their impact on diagnoses are unknown. What this study addsWhilst 99.7% of specimens were confirmed as gonorrhoea-negative, this study identified two confirmed and one suspected diagnostic escape mutants among 978 Xpert(R) NG-negative specimens, from two sexual health services. These findings demonstrate that Xpert(R) NG escape mutants are present in clinic attendees in England, and may result in missed gonorrhoea diagnoses How this study might affect research, practice or policyThe findings from this study support surveillance for diagnostic escape mutants and further studies to establish their prevalence and clinical impact.

papers.title: SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and vulnerability of human blastocysts during in vitro preimplantation development.
papers.abstract: Human preimplantation embryos express the SARS-CoV-2 entry factors ACE2, TMPRSS2 and BSG (CD147) on trophectoderm (TE) cells, suggesting susceptibility to infection. Likewise, SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped reporter viruses induced cytopathic effects in blastocysts, while the zona pellucida (ZP) appeared to confer partial protection. The impact of authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection on embryonic lineage specification and developmental competence has not been established. Here, we exposed cryopreserved human embryos, donated under ethics approval and informed consent, to authentic SARS-CoV-2 (B.1.617.2, Delta variant). While embryos with an intact ZP remained uninfected, laser-assisted hatching rendered 19/21 (90.5%) of embryos susceptible to infection, as confirmed by detection of viral dsRNA. Moreover, SARS-CoV-2 infection had a pronounced effect on blastocyst development with a possibly fatal outcome. Compared to mock-treated embryos (n = 47), infected blastocysts (n = 48) showed a significantly reduced surface area (p = 0.0003), reduced total cell number (p = 0.0139), and reduced NANOG+ epiblast cell numbers (p = 0.0054) 24 hours post-exposure, while the number of GATA4+ primitive endoderm cells remained unaffected (p = 0.5255). Intriguingly, despite viral replication being largely confined to the trophectoderm (TE), this selective epiblast reduction suggests a disruption of TE-derived paracrine signaling required for epiblast specification. Finally, prolonged viral replication resulted in embryonic lysis and death. Digital transcriptomic profiling (mock, n = 29 embryos; SARS-CoV-2, n = 28 embryos; each in n = 5 minipools) revealed upregulation of innate antiviral and inflammatory genes, including IFIH1, IRF7, NOD2, and TNFRSF1A, as well as the recently identified SARS-CoV-2 entry factor TMEM106B, alongside altered developmental signatures concerning genome activation, pluripotency, and lineage-specific programs. These findings show that ZP disruption makes human blastocysts susceptible to productive SARS-CoV-2 infection, with adverse consequences for lineage allocation and direct implications for biosafety and virological counselling in medically assisted reproduction practice. papers.title: The Lived Experiences of Long-Term Users of Copper-T Intrauterine Devices: A phenomenological Qualitative Study among women at Kawempe National Referral Hospital in Uganda
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Copper-T intrauterine device (Cu-T IUD) is a highly effective, non- hormonal, long-acting reversible contraceptive that can protect against pregnancy for up to 12 years, with a failure rate under 1%. Despite its clinical efficacy, early discontinuation remains a substantial challenge in Uganda, where discontinuation is approximated at 29% within the first year of use. Understanding the experiences of women using the Cu-T IUD is important to predict factors associated with discontinuation and to inform practice. MethodsBetween September and November 2025, we conducted twenty in-depth interviews with women of reproductive age (15-49 years) who had used a Cu-T IUD for at least two years, recruited from the family planning clinic of Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Kampala, Uganda. Data were analysed thematically, guided by the Social-Ecological Model and Lazarus and Folkmans Transactional Model of Stress and Coping. ResultsLong-term Cu-T IUD users reported both positive and negative experiences shaped by individual, interpersonal, and community factors. Two themes were identified at the individual-level domain: experiences during insertion and post-insertion experiences. Negative experiences, particularly heavy menstrual bleeding, anxiety, and abdominal pain, were common and distressing. Participants employed coping strategies, including taking painkillers, using home remedies, and resting, to manage these challenges with Cu-T IUD use. ConclusionsNegative experiences of Cu-T IUD are common among long-term users; womens coping strategies such as taking painkillers lead to continued use. Client-centred pre- insertion counselling addressing both anticipated side effects and common misconceptions, alongside accessible follow-up services, may facilitate long-term Cu-T IUD use.

papers.title: Feasibility and Acceptability of a Prospective Remote Pilot Study for Assessment of Airborne Environmental Exposures and Male Fertility
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of serial biosampling and environmental exposure assessment in reproductive-aged men and compare participant experiences with in-person versus remote sample collection. DesignProspective cohort pilot study. SubjectsEighteen healthy men aged 21-44 years with no history of infertility, medical conditions or medications known to cause infertility, or prior scrotal or testicular surgery. ExposureIndoor and personal environmental exposure monitoring using PurpleAir monitors and Fresh Air wristbands, respectively. Main Outcome MeasuresFeasibility of repeated remote semen and blood collection, evaluated by participant retention and number of samples returned, and participant-reported acceptability, ease of use, discomfort, preference for at-home versus in-clinic sampling, and willingness to participate in longitudinal studies. Results18 participants completed the initial in-person and scheduled at-home sampling, and 16 (89%) completed subsequent remote sampling. Participants successfully collected and shipped serial capillary blood samples using homeRNA and semen samples using the Fellow Semen Analysis Kit. Participants rated both collection methods as easy to use and reported minimal discomfort with blood collection. At-home participation was preferred over in-clinic sampling, particularly for semen collection. All 16 participants completing the final survey reported willingness to participate in a similar study again. Participants were willing to provide a median of 18 semen samples (range, 2-40) and 18 blood samples (range, 5-40) over a future hypothetical study. Both home-based environmental monitoring approaches were well accepted. ConclusionSerial remote semen and blood collection paired with environmental exposure monitoring was feasible and acceptable among reproductive-aged men. High retention, preference for at-home sampling, and willingness to provide repeated samples support this approach for larger longitudinal studies investigating environmental exposures and male reproductive health.

papers.title: Integrating voluntary family planning and cervical cancer screening and preventative treatment: lessons from the MULHER study in Mozambique
papers.abstract: IntroductionMozambique faces a significant burden of cervical cancer, but screening rates are currently low. While voluntary family planning (vFP) services are more widely accessible, unmet need for contraception remains at 22%. Integrating vFP and cervical cancer screening and preventive therapy (CCS&PT) services presents an opportunity to address these issues by improving service efficiency and reaching more women. This paper examines the uptake, feasibility, and experiences of integrating vFP services into CCS&PT services in Mozambique. MethodsThis mixed-methods operational research study was conducted in four public health facilities in Mozambique. Quantitative data were collected from January 2020 to October 2022 as part of the MULHER study and included program monitoring data from clinical encounters (N=9,014) and client exit interviews (N=504). Qualitative data was gathered through in-depth interviews (IDIs) with 60 clients and 15 providers in two phases, in October 2021 and November 2022. ResultsOut of 9,014 women eligible for HPV screening, 88% received both HPV screening and vFP counselling. 21% of these women took up a modern method of FP, 20% of whom were new users. Multivariable analysis showed that the likelihood of receiving integrated services was significantly associated with a range of factors including parity, age and HIV status. Qualitative data revealed that both clients and providers generally perceived the integrated model as beneficial. Clients highlighted the convenience, enhanced privacy, reduced travel costs, and opportunity to learn about new services. Providers emphasized similar benefits alongside the potential for increased demand through peer referrals. ConclusionsIntegrating vFP into CCS&PT services in Mozambique has the potential to increase vFP uptake, including among new users. The integrated model proved feasible and acceptable to both women and providers. The findings support the scaling up of this model to improve access to vFP and CCS&PT services and enhance womens sexual and reproductive health. Teaser key messageIntegrating voluntary family planning into cervical cancer screening service provision in Mozambique results in high levels of satisfaction among patients and providers and appears to make FP methods available to new users. Key MessagesO_LIThe study shows high levels of uptake of integrated vFP services among women enrolled in cervical screening and preventive therapy (CCS&PT) in the four public health facilities in Maputo and Gaza provinces, with almost 9 in 10 women who were enrolled for HPV screening also receiving vFP counselling on the day of their visit. C_LIO_LIOffering vFP services to women who attend CCS&PT services in Mozambique is feasible and presents an opportunity for increased access to women with unmet needs; one in five of the women taking up a contraceptive method were new users. C_LIO_LIClients who accessed integrated services expressed a high degree of satisfaction with the convenience, enhanced privacy, reduced travel costs and opportunity to learn about new services that this model presents. C_LI

papers.title: TruBlk™ Shilajit Resin Improves Sexual Function in Men with Erectile Dysfunction: A Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Multicenter Trial
papers.abstract: Erectile dysfunction and age-related testosterone decline are common and growing concerns among ageing men, yet current pharmacological options are constrained by tolerability, cost, and reluctance to start hormone-based therapy, leaving a real gap for safe, long-term alternatives. Shilajit, a resinous plant exudate long used in Ayurvedic medicine, is increasingly proposed to fill this gap with its bioactive constituents thought to confer adaptogenic, antioxidant, and androgen-modulating effects. However, clinical support for this use remains thin, with most existing trials small and conducted in healthy men rather than those with diagnosed erectile dysfunction. In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial (CTRI/2025/07/090919), 100 men aged 35-55 years with mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction (IIEF erectile function domain score 11- 25) and symptoms suggestive of androgen deficiency were enrolled across two sites. Participants received 250 mg twice daily of standardised TruBlk Shilajit resin or matched placebo for 90 days. Primary endpoints, as registered, were change from baseline in IIEF total and domain scores, total and free testosterone and cortisol, and Hypogonadism Impact of Symptoms Questionnaire (HIS-Q) domain scores. Secondary endpoints included nitric oxide, Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), and Participant and Investigator Global Assessments. Semen parameters were assessed in a subset of participants. IIEF total score improved significantly more in the TruBlk group (+32.1% vs. +13.6%; d=0.67, p=0.005), with significant gains in four of the five domains, namely erectile function, orgasmic function, overall satisfaction, and intercourse satisfaction (d=0.52-0.61, p=0.011-0.044), while sexual desire showed a smaller, non-significant improvement (d=0.44, p=0.109). This was accompanied by significant increases in total testosterone (+46.1% vs. +10.0%; d=0.44, p=0.030) and free testosterone (+37.4% vs. +6.8%; d=0.41, p=0.048). HIS-Q symptom domains showed a similar pattern to IIEF, with Day 90 differences favouring TruBlk in three of five domains (sexual, energy, and sleep; d=-0.59 to -0.82, p<0.02), while cognition and mood showed smaller, non-significant differences (d=-0.46 to -0.49, p=0.06-0.10). Among secondary endpoints, fatigue fell substantially more with TruBlk than with placebo, with FSS scores decreasing by 51.8% vs. 27.4% from baseline, a large between-group effect at Day 90 (d=-1.13, p<0.0001). At Day 90, 56-58% of TruBlk participants were rated "Much" or "Very Much Improved" on global assessment, compared with 12-14% of placebo. Nitric oxide showed no significant between-group difference. In an exploratory semen-analysis subset (n=57), sperm concentration increased with TruBlk relative to placebo ({delta}=0.53, p<0.001), and in a subset of 40 participants assessed for motility, total motility ({delta}=0.63, p<0.001) and progressive motility (d=0.82, p=0.014) also improved. Ninety days of standardised TruBlk Shilajit resin improved erectile function and increased total and free testosterone in men with mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction, with improvement in several hypogonadism-related symptom domains, reduced fatigue and, in an exploratory subset, improved sperm concentration and motility. These results support standardised Shilajit resin as a promising intervention for sexual dysfunction in a clinically diagnosed population, meriting further clinical evaluation.

papers.title: Covering all the BASEs? Barriers and facilitators to STI testing among international students living in England
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe emergence in England of ceftriaxone-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the bacteria which causes gonorrhoea, is a public health concern. Most cases of ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhoea in England are travel-associated. We assessed the barriers and facilitators to sexually transmitted infection testing among international students living in England. MethodsWe conducted semi-structured interviews (March-August 2025) with international students attending a university in London. We recruited students through various university networks and snowball sampling. We used the Capability, Opportunity and Motivation (COM-B) model and conducted a thematic analysis. ResultsWe conducted 15 interviews. Most participants were from China (n=8) and Nigeria (n=2), with other participants from countries in Europe, Asia, the Middle East and the Americas. Most participants were 25-34 years old and in a postgraduate programme. Two-thirds of our sample had previously been tested for STIs (7 in England, and 3 in their home country). STI language and knowledge were key psychological capability barriers to STI testing, awareness of STI testing options was a facilitator. Under physical capability, no STI symptoms influenced testing for some, but prompted testing for others. Belief in confidentiality, privacy, and anonymity of testing, alongside perceived social and individual benefits of STI testing, were identified as facilitators under reflective motivation. Perceived risk varied based on relationship status. Anticipated judgement and stigma were the main social opportunity barriers, while trust in health professionals was the main facilitator. Fragmented services and poor proximity were key physical opportunity barriers; perceived availability of services and access to free, straightforward testing were facilitators. ConclusionsWe integrated these findings into national STI public health messaging targeted at university students in the England. The findings can be used to create culturally appropriate resources to raise awareness of STI-related symptoms and, among those with a need, promote STI testing.

papers.title: Determinants of Emergency Contraceptive Use among Adolescent Girls aged 15-19 Years in West Asembo Ward, Rarieda Sub County, Siaya County, Kenya: A Mixed method, Cross-sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Despite high uptake of conventional contraceptive services, adolescent pregnancies remain high in West Asembo ward, Siaya County, Kenya. This study determined the utilization, factors associated with use, and perceptions towards emergency contraception (EC) among adolescent girls in this region. A cross-sectional study design using a mixed-methods approach was employed. Quantitatively, 400 female adolescents aged 15-19 years were randomly sampled using stratified sampling across five sub-locations. Data were collected via interviewer-administered electronic questionnaires. Qualitatively, ten purposively selected Key Informant Interviews were conducted with healthcare and pharmaceutical providers, alongside four Focus Group Discussions with adolescents in sub-locations representing the highest and lowest teenage pregnancy rates. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics (=0.05) in SPSS v.29, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis in NVivo 14 before triangulation. Results showed that 34.8% of the respondents had ever used emergency contraception. In the bivariate analysis, being aged 18-19 years significantly reduced the likelihood of EC use compared to those aged 15-17 years (COR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.21-0.50, p < 0.0001). Lower primary education was associated with a lower likelihood of EC use compared to no formal education (COR: 0.04, 95% CI: 0.003-0.49, p = 0.012). Crucially, adolescent girls who were single and living alone were significantly more likely to use ECs than single counterparts living with parents or guardians (COR: 5.23, 95% CI: 2.86-9.56, p < 0.0001). In conclusion, emergency contraceptive use among adolescent girls in West Asembo Ward is relatively low. The findings underscore the need for a comprehensive, adolescent-centered approach involving health facilities, schools, community health promoters, and private pharmacies to empower adolescents with accurate information while ensuring confidential, accessible EC services coupled with reproductive health counseling.

papers.title: Factors associated with cervical cancer stigma among women living in urban Nepal
papers.abstract: Cervical cancer stigma can affect perceptions of cancer, interactions with affected people, and engagement in preventive behavior. Evidence on factors associated with cervical cancer stigma among women in urban Nepal is limited. This study examined sociodemographic, reproductive and knowledge-related factors associated with cervical cancer stigma. We analysed baseline data from 310 women aged 30-60 years enrolled in a community-based, two-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial in Budanilkantha Municipality, Kathmandu, Nepal, between 15 June and 15 December 2022. Cervical cancer stigma was assessed using the validated Nepali version of the Cancer Stigma Scale. Multivariable generalized estimating equations (GEE) with a Gaussian distribution and identity link were used to examine associations, adjusting for age, ethnicity, religion, education, occupation, and annual household income. Results are reported as beta coefficients ({beta}) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The mean age was 41.5 years, and 54.2% of participants were Janjati. Overall, 82.3% had heard of cervical cancer, 31.8% knew its signs and symptoms, and 1.6% had heard of Human Papilloma Virus. Most knew cervical cancer could be prevented (75.6%) and treated (90.1%). After adjustment, Janjati women ({beta} = 0.311, 95% CI: 0.099, 0.523) and women from other ethnic groups, including Dalit and Madhesi ({beta} = 0.411, 95% CI: 0.054, 0.768), had higher cervical cancer stigma scores than Brahmin/Chettri women. Formal education was associated with lower cervical cancer stigma scores ({beta} = -0.359, 95% CI: - 0.554, -0.165). Homemakers ({beta} = 0.263, 95% CI: 0.014, 0.513) and self-employed women ({beta} = 0.309, 95% CI: 0.054, 0.564) had higher cervical cancer stigma scores than salaried women. Awareness of cervical cancer ({beta} = -0.249, 95% CI: -0.437, -0.060), its signs and symptoms ({beta} = - 0.245, 95% CI: -0.465, -0.025), preventability ({beta} = -0.285, 95% CI: -0.554, -0.016) and treatability ({beta} = -0.362, 95% CI: -0.635, -0.089) was associated with lower cervical cancer stigma scores. Age, religion, income, risk-factor awareness, menopause history, number of pregnancies and use of Intra Uterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCD) use were not significantly associated with cervical cancer stigma. Cervical cancer stigma among women in urban Nepal was associated with educational status, ethnicity, employment, and specific aspects of cervical cancer knowledge. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine whether improving cancer knowledge can effectively reduce cervical cancer stigma.

papers.title: Functional analysis of NANOS protein variants identified in men with infertility employing zebrafish embryos
papers.abstract: Study questionAre vertebrate NANOS proteins associated with human fertility, and can a rapid in vivo assay in zebrafish be established to evaluate the biological activity of human NANOS variants? Summary answerCombining a rapid in vivo assay we developed for Nanos protein activity and patient-derived genetic data, we identified NANOS variants that could contribute to male infertility. What is known alreadyMale infertility affects approximately 17% of the population, but linking specific gene variants to this condition remains challenging. NANOS proteins are essential regulators of germ cell development in different model organisms; however, a rapid and robust in vivo assay for evaluating their activity in the context of human male infertility is currently lacking. Study design, size, durationExome/genome data from 3,338 men included in the Male Reproductive Genomics (MERGE) cohort were examined in this study. Of these, 2038 men showed severely impaired spermatogenesis but were otherwise healthy. Ninety-Six men with intact spermatogenesis were included in the study as controls. Additionally, the study included a targeted analysis of NANOS variants in 44 patients from the IMIGC cohort. Participants/materials, setting, methodsThe exome/genome data were screened for rare, stop-gain, frameshift, splice site, as well as missense variants in NANOS1, NANOS2, and NANOS3. Human amino acid substitutions were introduced at the corresponding positions in the zebrafish proteins. Ectopic co-expression of wild-type Dnd1 and Nanos3 in zebrafish embryos induces a germ cell-like fate in somatic cells, resulting in severe developmental defects and embryonic lethality. Based on this principle, we established a rapid in vivo assay in which wild-type Dnd1 was co-expressed with wild-type or variant Nanos2 and Nanos3 proteins in live zebrafish embryos, expecting early embryonic death if a variant protein is functional. This assay was used to evaluate the activity of NANOS2 and NANOS3 variants identified in men with infertility. Main results and the role of chanceIn human exome/genome sequencing data, we identified one heterozygous missense variant in NANOS2 and two heterozygous missense variants in NANOS3. The function of the variants was examined in the zebrafish using the in vivo assay we developed. Co-expression of wild-type Dnd1 with selected Nanos2 or Nanos3 variants identified in infertile men resulted in defects in induction of the germ cell-like phenotype, demonstrating the power of the biological readout for evaluating the potential effects of patient-derived variants on NANOS protein activity. Together, our analysis enabled the evaluation of single nucleotide variants, whose impact on protein function is difficult to predict, and allowed us to distinguish variants with little or no effect on protein function from those that strongly reduce activity and may potentially contribute to infertility. Limitations, reasons for cautionThe assay requires access to zebrafish embryos and basic imaging equipment. Although the functional conservation of NANOS proteins between zebrafish and humans is supported by previous studies, species-specific differences may influence protein activity. Therefore, the zebrafish assay should be considered one component of a broader framework for evaluating NANOS variants as contributing factor for infertility. Wider implications of the findingsUsing NANOS2 and NANOS3 as examples, we demonstrate that integrating clinical genetic data with functional cell and developmental biology can help establish links between candidate disease genes and human fertility. This strategy may apply to other germline-specific genes whose ectopic expression produces measurable developmental phenotypes in zebrafish embryos. Study funding/competing interest(s)We acknowledge the support from the Spanish Ministry of Health Instituto Carlos III-FIS FONDOS FEDER (grant number PI23/00425), the German Research Foundation (DFG) grants to E.R. (RA 863/17-1, RA 863/18-1), to E.R., C.F., and F.T. (Clinical Research Unit Male Germ Cells, CRU 326, project number 329621271), to S.K., C.F., and F.T. (Collaborative Research Centre Reproduction.MS, SFB 1748, project number 549467913), the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR) Junior Scientist Research Centre ReproTrack.MS to S.K. and F.T. (project number 01GR2303), and funding from the Medical Faculty of the University of Munster. The authors declare no competing interests Trial registration numberN/A.

papers.title: Health workers and administrators experiences of duty handover on maternity wards in public health facilities in Hoima District, Uganda: a qualitative phenomenological study
papers.abstract: BackgroundDuty handover is a high-risk point in the continuity of maternity care, and breakdowns in handover communication have been linked to delayed care and avoidable harm. Qualitative evidence from maternity wards in low-resource Sub-Saharan African settings is limited, and to our knowledge no study has examined handover experiences on maternity wards in Hoima District, Uganda. This study explored the experiences and challenges of health workers and administrators regarding duty handover on maternity wards in public health facilities in Hoima District, Uganda. MethodsWe conducted a qualitative phenomenological study. Fifteen in-depth interviews with maternity ward health workers and five key informant interviews with administrators were carried out across six public health facilities. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using a modified Colaizzi seven-step method. Reflexivity and bracketing were addressed through a pre-fieldwork assumptions statement and bracketing interview, a reflexive journal kept throughout data collection, and independent double-coding of a subset of transcripts. ResultsTwo themes were identified: duty handover practices on maternity wards, and challenges experienced by health workers during handover. Handover was inconsistent in structure, duration and adherence to protocol, and relied heavily on informal telephone communication rather than structured face-to-face reporting. Standardised tools were used in some facilities only. Participants identified time constraints and workload, inadequate training, limited resources and supervision, negative staff attitudes, and difficulty accessing patient information as key challenges, and linked communication breakdowns to delays and errors in care. Patients and families were largely not involved in handover. ConclusionsDuty handover on the maternity wards studied was inconsistent and constrained by capability-, opportunity- and motivation-related barriers operating together. Standardised and locally adapted handover tools, targeted training, stronger supervision and facility- and national-level guidance appear necessary to protect continuity of care in comparable low-resource maternity settings.

papers.title: Trends in, and factors associated with, chemsex in a community sample of gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men in England, 2022-2025
papers.abstract: BackgroundChemsex, drug use before/during sex to facilitate and enhance the experience, is undertaken by a minority of gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM), but evidence of chemsex prevalence in England is limited. This study describes trends in chemsex prevalence between 2022-2025 and identifies factors associated with chemsex amongst GBMSM in England. MethodsData from the RiiSH study (2022-2025), an annual online cross-sectional survey of GBMSM recruited through social networking/dating apps and community partners, were analysed. Trends in chemsex prevalence and adjusted prevalence were estimated using log-binomial regression models. The following seven variables were candidate factors associated with chemsex and were assessed through logistic regression: age, sexual orientation, education, employment, HIV status, HIV PrEP use, and sexual health service (SHS) use. Results5728 GBMSM were included in this study. Adjusted chemsex prevalence varied from 6.1% in 2022 to 4.2% in 2023, 5.1% in 2024 and 6.8% in 2025. Chemsex was more likely in GBMSM who were: gay (aOR=1.57 versus other sexual orientations; 95%CI 1.11-2.29, p=0.01), unemployed (aOR=3.08 versus employed full-time; 95%CI 2.19-4.26, p<0.001); aged 35-59 versus 16-34 years (p<0.001), with recent HIV PrEP use (aOR=3.79 versus no recent use; 95%CI 2.63-5.56, p<0.001), SHS use (aOR=2.23 versus no recent use; 95%CI 1.76-2.83, p<0.001), and living with HIV (aOR=3.16 versus negative/unknown HIV status; 95%CI 2.43-4.09, p<0.001). ConclusionsChemsex prevalence was low and stable between 2022-2025. PrEP and SHS use were associated with chemsex, supporting integration of specialist support services within SHS.

papers.title: How healthcare professionals manage uncertainty around hormone replacement therapy (dis-)continuation: the TAPER qualitative Study
papers.abstract: Many women experience menopausal symptoms after stopping hormone replacement therapy (HRT). An evidence gap remains regarding how women and healthcare professionals (HCPs) make decisions about discontinuing and restarting HRT. AimTo explore experiences of HCPs that support women when they discontinue and restart HRT. Design and settingQualitative study with HCPs working in NHS primary care. Method*The model describes HCPs experiences of supporting women to discontinue HRT as an iterative process characterised by uncertainty. Discussions about discontinuation were commonly prompted by changes in clinical risk or annual HRT review, but decisions about whether and when to stop also depended on womens symptoms, side effects, life stage and readiness. HCPs described agreeing an individualised discontinuation strategy, providing support during the process, and reviewing women afterwards to consider alternative treatments or, where appropriate, restarting HRT. Semi-structured interviews with HCPs (n = 15) conducted between October 2025 and March 2026. A preliminary coding template was created using the discussion guide as a framework. Each interview was then coded inductively against the template which developed iteratively. Team based discussion helped refine codes into themes and sub-themes, and a subsequent conceptual model was created. ResultsThe model describes HCPs experiences of supporting women to discontinue HRT as an iterative process characterised by uncertainty. Discussions about discontinuation were commonly prompted by changes in clinical risk or annual HRT review, but decisions about whether and when to stop also depended on womens symptoms, side effects, life stage and readiness. HCPs described agreeing an individualised discontinuation strategy, providing support during the process, and reviewing women after discontinuation to consider alternative treatments or, where appropriate, restarting HRT. ConclusionHCPs recognise the importance of readiness to discontinue and that decision making should be woman led, with HCP support, clear practice guidance and opportunities to revisit treatment. Further research is needed to support women weigh up their personalised risk and benefit of continuing/discontinuing and identify discontinuation strategies that limit resurgent symptoms. How this fits inO_LIHormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) use has increased substantially, but little is known about how healthcare professionals support women who are considering discontinuation. C_LIO_LIExisting guidance offers limited evidence on when and how HRT should be stopped or how best to manage recurrent symptoms. C_LIO_LIThis study shows that discontinuation is an iterative, individualised process shaped by clinical risk, symptoms, life stage and womens readiness to stop. C_LIO_LIHealthcare professionals would benefit from clearer guidance to support shared decision-making, follow-up and decisions about alternative treatment or restarting HRT. C_LI

papers.title: Menstrual health, food insecurity, and protection vulnerability among adolescent girls in internally displaced persons camps in Benue State, Nigeria: A focused ethnographic study
papers.abstract: Adolescent girls living in internally displaced persons (IDP) camps manage menstruation amid food insecurity, inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), disrupted education, gendered social norms and protection systems. These challenges are often addressed through separate humanitarian programmes, obscuring how they interact in girls everyday lives. This study explored menstrual-health experiences and perceived nutritional deprivation among adolescent girls in five IDP camps in Benue State, Nigeria. We conducted a focused ethnographic qualitative study in the International Market, Mega, Ortese, Uikpam, and Abagana camps. Twenty-five in-depth interviews with menstruating adolescent girls aged 13-19 years were complemented by focus group discussions with adolescent girls, adult women, adult men, and camp leaders, and structured WASH and food observations. Interviews and discussions were conducted in English, Tiv or both, transcribed verbatim and translated where necessary. Data were managed in MAXQDA and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Frequencies describe the distribution of 435 coded excerpts and are not participant prevalence estimates. Six themes and 20 subthemes were generated. Menstrual-health management and material constraints accounted for 95 coded excerpts (21.8%), followed by knowledge and lived experience (80; 18.4%), food insecurity and perceived nutritional deprivation (70; 16.1%), coping and adaptive agency (70; 16.1%), sociocultural beliefs and taboos (65; 14.9%), and self-reported symptoms and participation restrictions (55; 12.6%). Girls described irregular access to commercial pads, reliance on improvised materials, limited water and soap, and toilets that were unsafe or inaccessible at night. Dietary monotony, meal skipping, and hunger were perceived to intensify pain, weakness, and fatigue. Fear of staining, menstrual silence, and household restrictions contributed to withdrawal from school, livelihood, and domestic activities. Peer support was protective, but some girls undertook informal work to obtain menstrual materials, raising safeguarding concerns. Menstrual health in prolonged displacement is not an isolated hygiene issue but an outcome of interacting material, nutritional, sociocultural, educational, and protection constraints. Humanitarian responses should combine predictable access to acceptable menstrual materials with safe WASH facilities, adolescent-responsive food and nutrition support, confidential health services, community education and safeguarding mechanisms. Reported symptoms and nutritional experiences were not clinically measured.

papers.title: Menopause timing, epigenetic aging and blood-cell traits
papers.abstract: Menopause timing links reproductive lifespan with later-life health, motivating investigation of its molecular and hematological correlates. We combined Generation Scotland analyses of women sampled at or after reported menopause (n = 1,444) and initially menstruating women followed for GP-ascertained menopause onset (n = 1,725; 251 events) with bidirectional and multivariable Mendelian randomization. Higher age-adjusted GrimAge V1, GrimAge V2 and DunedinPACE corresponded to 0.34-0.40 years earlier menopause per SD in the retrospective cohort at nominal P < 0.05. Prospective associations were nonsignificant, and cohort and primary bidirectional aging-related genetic associations did not survive multiple-testing correction. Genetically predicted later menopause was associated with higher neutrophil percentage and count and lower lymphocyte percentage in women; these associations and female-male contrasts survived correction. CRP conditional on menopause timing was associated with higher GrimAge and PhenoAge acceleration and shorter leukocyte telomere length after correction. None of 36 estimated inflammatory indirect effects reached P < 0.05. These findings highlight blood-cell composition as a prominent correlate of reproductive timing and identify selected methylation-aging signatures for further study. Together, they position reproductive-hematological relationships as a specific avenue for understanding the connection between menopause and systemic aging.

papers.title: Endocrine and well-being profiles shape psychosexual health and menopausal symptoms after menopause
papers.abstract: Menopause is a major neuroendocrine transition characterised by substantial changes in endocrine milieu, physiological, psychological, and psychosexual health. Although menopausal symptoms are common, their range and severity vary considerably between individuals, suggesting that menopause is a multifaceted process. Endocrine markers (luteinising, follicle-stimulating & anti-Mullerian hormone), together with perceived well-being, may contribute to this variability. Thus, the aim was to capture the complex impact of endocrine and well-being markers on psychosexual health and menopausal symptoms. Therefore, we first applied principal component analyses to identify individual endocrine and well-being profiles, to then assess their association with psychosexual health and psychophysiological symptoms in pre- and post-menopausal females. Post-compared to pre-menopausal females report reduced psychosexual health and greater urogenital and psychological symptom burden. Endocrine and well-being profiles interact with reproductive status: Post-menopausal females with lower subjective well-being and a stronger menopause-like endocrine milieu report decreased overall psychosexual health and more sexual related pain. Additionally, endocrine milieu interacted with reproductive status on urogenital symptoms: Post-menopausal females with a stronger menopause-like endocrine milieu report less urogenital symptoms.

papers.title: An insight into birthing and EmONC service utilisation for making birthing safe: a qualitative study in underdeveloped districts of Punjab, Pakistan.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe qualitative study was conducted to understand the socio-cultural factors (challenges and enabling factors) those influence the decisions and ability of the pregnant women and their families to make better use of the available safe birthing and EmONC services in two districts (Khanewal and Jhang) of Punjab, Pakistan. ObjectivesTo explore the key social, personal and professional considerations (factors) that influence the women (and family) decision and ability to utilise various birthing and EMONC services and to understand care providers interest and ability to offer these safe birthing services in the districts of Jhang and Khanewal in Pakistan. Study DesignThe qualitative study was conducted, during the year 2013/14, on three rural health centers and two district headquarter hospitals in Kanewal and Jhang districts in Punjab. Through purposive sampling, 42 registered clients were interviewed to explain the different birthing experience along with 15 service providers, 2 district level programme managers and 2 transport vendors. The collected qualitative data from interviews were transcribed, and key emerging concepts/ themes were identified. A range and continuum of coded responses/ comments were compiled and discussed under each theme. ResultsMain themes were structured birth planning; antenatal at health centres; skilled birth attendance; emergency obstetric and neonatal care (EmONC); and EmONC travel. The study found that pregnant women consult their husbands and mother in laws for taking birthing decisions; consult the skilled birth attendant for management of complication; private clinics are preferred for various social and logistic reasons; many private clinics doing caesarean are not adequately equipped; male reluctance (for cultural reasons) to make in-advance transport arrangement for possible EmONC; travel voucher utilisation remained low because of limited coverage and less-friendly procedures. ConclusionSafe birthing decisions could be complex; and influenced by multiple social, cultural, economic, service access and quality considerations. Safe birthing practices can be improved if interventions remain sensitive to these preferences and realities.

papers.title: Strategies for sustaining sexual and reproductive health services during recurrent flooding in Adamawa State, Nigeria. A qualitative study.
papers.abstract: Seasonal flooding in Adamawa State, Nigeria damages health facilities, breaks supply chains, and displaces health workers and communities, while increasing health needs. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services are often deprioritized, yet evidence on how they are sustained remains limited. We examined how SRH services were sustained during recurrent flooding. We conducted a qualitative descriptive study in the flood-prone Local Government Areas of Numan and Fufore. We held eight focus group discussions with women and girls and 20 key informant interviews with health providers, supply chain actors, and program implementers. Flooding closed or damaged health facilities, broke supply and cold chains, and displaced health workers. Participants linked these disruptions to unattended births and to rising hemorrhage, stillbirth, miscarriage, and genital infections. Service continuity depended less on the formal health system than on anticipatory, community-led adaptation across three phases. Before floods, stakeholders mapped risk, pre-positioned commodities, trained women in contraceptive self-injection, and dispensed medicines in advance. During floods, care shifted to mobile outreach, task-sharing, transport by canoe and boat, and community-led referral. Community health workers, traditional birth attendants, Ward Development Committees, and womens groups reached cut-off communities. Across seasons, adaptations evolved toward cash transfers, savings groups, local reusable-pad production, and decentralized commodity hubs. Continuity relied heavily on unpaid community labor and womens own resources. Sustaining SRH services in flood-prone settings requires institutionalized preparedness, decentralized supply, empowered communities, and protected health financing. Community-led models offer a transferable approach to health security in a changing climate.

papers.title: Antibiotic treatment of asymptomatic urogenital infections in infertile couples is associated with improved sperm quality including sperm apoptosis parameters
papers.abstract: BackgroundEuropean Association of Urology (EAU) Guidelines identify urogenital infections as a possible treatable cause of infertility, yet the current recommendation for antibiotic treatment remains weak due to a lack of high-quality evidence. We evaluated the effect of antibiotic treatment of asymptomatic urogenital infections on both conventional and apoptosis-related (flow cytometry sperm apoptosis test, FACS-APO) sperm parameters, as well as on pregnancy outcomes, in infertile couples. MethodsIn this retrospective, single-centre study, we analysed 265 couples with an asymptomatic urogenital infection (Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma hominis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Chlamydia trachomatis) confirmed in at least one partner by first-void urine testing, who received simultaneous antibiotic treatment. Paired conventional semen analysis and FACS-APO were performed before and 0-9 months after treatment completion. Partner infection concordance, the effect of follow-up timing on treatment response, and pregnancy outcomes within 12 months were also assessed. ResultsSperm concentration, total sperm count, total and progressive motility, and the proportion of viable sperm increased significantly after treatment, while the proportion of late apoptotic / necrotic sperm and calculated sperm DNA fragmentation decreased significantly (all p<0.05); the proportion of early apoptotic sperm remained unchanged, and semen volume did not change. Among 244 couples with complete bilateral microbiological testing, Ureaplasma urealyticum was by far the most prevalent pathogen (57.8% of men, 87.7% of women), and female partner positivity given male positivity was 83.0%. The improvement in sperm concentration and total sperm count was most pronounced within 3 months after treatment and diminished, or reversed, beyond 6 months. Pregnancy was achieved in 127 of 265 couples (47.9%; per-protocol rate 53.4%) within 12 months, most commonly following in vitro fertilization (72/127) or spontaneously (21/127). ConclusionsAntibiotic treatment of asymptomatic urogenital infections in infertile couples was associated with significant improvement in conventional semen parameters and a reduction in sperm apoptosis and calculated DNA fragmentation. Given the retrospective, uncontrolled design, these findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive proof of a causal, fertility-enhancing effect, and warrant confirmation in prospective controlled studies.
